channel.title: A writing desk for working a draft over on WRITEpad
channel.description: Recent content in A writing desk for working a draft over on WRITEpad

item.title: Export
item.description:
Export (top bar) writes out the manuscript you have open, as it stands: its pages in outline order, the ★ live version of each, and none of the pages left out of the cut. With a note open instead, it exports the note.

Formats

Format Good for
Word (.docx) Word, Pages and Google Docs; sending to an editor or agent
PDF Print-ready, 5.5 × 8.5 inch pages
EPUB E-readers
OpenDocument (.odt) LibreOffice
Rich Text (.rtf) Opens almost anywhere
Web page (.html) Reading in a browser or posting online
Markdown Other writing tools
Plain text Anything
MP3 audiobook One narrated file per chapter; a screenplay is read by its cast

Word, OpenDocument and Rich Text files get a title page with your byline, and each chapter starts on a new page. Page properties are never exported.

item.title: Listen and table reads
item.description:
Hearing a draft catches what reading it silently misses: clunky rhythm, repeated words, dialogue nobody would say. WRITEpad reads your work aloud with voices that run on your own computer. Nothing is sent anywhere to be read.

Listen

Put the cursor where you want to start and click ▶ Listen (⌘↵), or select a passage to hear just that. The sentence being read lights up as it goes. Esc stops.

item.title: Pages and chapters
item.description:
A manuscript is made of pages: chapters, scenes or sections, whatever suits the book. Open a manuscript from the Manuscripts tab and its outline appears in the sidebar, one row per page in book order.

Each row shows the page’s title. If the page has more than one version, the row also shows how many, and which one is live, such as 2 · Jacobs 1902.

item.title: Your first vault
item.description:
WRITEpad keeps everything in a vault: an ordinary folder on your computer. Notes are plain markdown files you could open in any editor, including Obsidian. Manuscripts, their versions and your settings for them live in a .writepad folder inside it. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Shortcuts on these pages say ⌘. On Windows, use Ctrl.

item.title: Your story world
item.description:
The World tab keeps your story bible: characters, locations, relationships, things, and an overview of the world itself. Each entry is an ordinary markdown note in your vault (under world/), so you can write as much or as little about it as you like.

Add an entry

Each group on the World tab (Characters, Locations and so on) has a + button. Pick the Type, give it a Name and click Create. The new note opens, ready for a description.

item.title: Library and targets
item.description:
The Library measures published books so you can see how your draft compares: how long their chapters run, how long their sentences are, how much is dialogue, how chapters end. Blend the ones you admire into a target, and WRITEpad measures every page you write against it.

Only the numbers are kept, never the books’ text.

Add books

On the Library tab, click Add books… and pick EPUB files. Each one is measured and added to the list.

item.title: Settings and updates
item.description:
Click Settings at the top right. Changes take effect when you click Save.

Vault

The folder WRITEpad works in. Change… opens a different one. See Your first vault.

Narration

  • Set up narration installs the voices (about 350 MB, needs Python 3.10 or newer).
  • Voice for italic lines: the second voice, for thoughts and other italics.
  • Pause after paragraphs (seconds).

If you already have Kokoro installed, point Python with kokoro-onnx and Kokoro model folder at it instead. See Listen and table reads.

item.title: The writing desk at a glance
item.description:
With a manuscript open, WRITEpad has four parts.

The top bar

  • The vault’s name (top left): click it to open a different vault. Beside it, words today counts what you’ve written today across every page and note (cutting words counts against it).
  • 🎙 Dictate: talk and the words land at the cursor. See Dictation.
  • ▶ Listen: reads aloud from the cursor, or just the selection (⌘↵). Esc stops. Next to it are the narrator voice and the speed. See Listen and table reads.
  • Export: Word, PDF, EPUB and more. See Export.
  • Settings: your vault, narration, theme, dictation and updates. See Settings.
  • ?: opens the help page for what you’re looking at, in your browser. The Help menu (⌘?) does the same, and has the blog and Report a bug….

Each panel on the right has a small ? beside its heading that opens the help page for that panel.

item.title: Timeline
item.description:
The Timeline lists your story’s events in the order they happen, which isn’t always the order you tell them. Each event links to the scenes where the reader sees it, so flashbacks, cold opens and narrators who disagree are easy to spot.

Click Timeline on the World tab.

Add events

  • + Event at the start adds the first event.
  • + between two events adds one there.
  • From a page, + Event here (in In this scene) adds an event linked to that page.

Give it a Name and, if you like, a When in story time (“the next morning”, “Fri Apr 26 2041, 8:14am”).

item.title: Versions of a page
item.description:
Every page can have several versions (takes). Try a tighter opening, a different point of view or a new ending without losing what you had. The versions sit side by side above the text.

Fork a version

Click + Fork (Copy this version to try something different). WRITEpad copies the version you’re looking at and opens the copy, compared against the original (see Onion skin). Rewrite the copy; the original stays exactly as it was.

item.title: Notes and links
item.description:
Notes are plain markdown files in your vault: research, ideas, outlines, anything that isn’t the book itself. They work in any markdown editor, and the same folder can be an Obsidian vault at the same time.

Write a note

On the Notes tab, click New note and give it a Name. A name with a slash, like ideas/Unit 12, puts the note in a folder. It opens ready to type, and saves as you go.

item.title: Onion skin: compare versions
item.description:
Onion skin lays one version of a page over the one you’re reading. Words you added are tinted. Words the other version had are drawn as faint ghosts, struck through, right where they were. You read the new version and see the old one underneath.

Compare two versions

Open a page with more than one version. In the Onion skin panel on the right, pick a version under Compare with.

item.title: Cuts
item.description:
A cut is a named recipe for the whole book:

  1. Which pages are in it.
  2. What order they go in.
  3. Which version (★ live take) of each page it uses.

You might keep a cut of the original draft, one for each revision pass, a shorter cut for a contest with a word limit, or one per narrator. Switching between them takes one click, and none of them ever deletes anything.

item.title: Comments
item.description:
Comments are notes about the text that aren’t part of it: “is this the house’s name or the street’s?”, “cut this?”, “check the date”. They sit in the Comments panel on the right, and the words they’re about are highlighted in the page. They’re never exported and never change your text.

Add one

Select some words, then click + Comment on selection (or press ⌘⌥M). Type your note and press Enter. Shift+Enter starts a new line in the note; Esc cancels.

item.title: Page properties
item.description:
Properties are your own notes about a page, as name and value pairs: point of view, setting, a date, a status, the source verses for a retelling. They sit under the page title and are never exported with the book.

Add one

Click + Property (Add to this page: verses, POV, setting, [[a note]]). Type a name, press Tab, type the value and press Enter. Names you’ve used on other pages are suggested as you type, so the same field stays spelled the same way.

item.title: Search
item.description:
The search box at the top of the sidebar looks through the whole vault: every note, every version of every page (not just the live ones), and page properties.

Search

Click the box, or press ⌘⇧F, and type. Results appear as you type.

  • Several words find places that have all of them.
  • Each result shows the page or note, where it is, and the matching text with your words highlighted.
  • Results with your words in the title, or the exact phrase, come first.

Click a result to open it, with the first match selected. Enter opens the top result. Esc clears the search.

item.title: History
item.description:
History keeps snapshots of the whole vault: every note and every version of every page, as they were. You can compare a page with any snapshot, restore one page, or roll the whole vault back.

It uses git under the hood, so the history also works with any git tool. You don’t need to know git to use it.

Turn it on

In the History panel on the right, click Turn on history. It’s off until you do, once per vault.

item.title: Screenplays
item.description:
WRITEpad writes screenplays as well as prose. A screenplay is a manuscript whose pages are scenes.

Start one

On the Manuscripts tab, click New…, pick Screenplay, give it a title and click Create.

Write

Type, and press Tab to change a line’s type: scene heading, action, character, dialogue and so on. The formatting bar reminds you: Screenplay · Tab changes a line’s type · ▶ Listen for a table read.

item.title: Dictation
item.description:
🎙 Dictate turns speech into text at the cursor. Transcription runs on your own computer with Whisper.

Dictate

Open a page or a note and put the cursor where the words should go. Then either:

  • Hold Right ⌥ (the Option key on the right; Right Alt on Windows) and talk. Let go, and the text lands at the cursor.
  • Tap it, or click 🎙 Dictate, to go hands-free: it keeps listening until you tap again.

The button shows ● Listening while it records and … Writing while it transcribes. Pressing another key while holding Right ⌥ cancels.

item.title: How long should a chapter be? Measure the books you love
item.description:
Ask “how long should a chapter be?” and you’ll get the same answer every time: somewhere between 2,000 and 5,000 words, unless it isn’t. That’s true, and it doesn’t help you decide anything.

A better question is: how long are the chapters in the books yours will sit next to on the shelf? That you can measure.

Why the usual advice is so vague

Chapter length is a pacing tool, not a rule. Short chapters speed a reader up. Each break is a small reward and an easy “one more”. Long chapters slow a reader down and let a scene breathe. Thrillers lean short. Literary fiction and epic fantasy often run long. Middle-grade novels run short because the reader is younger and the book is shorter.

item.title: How to keep multiple versions of a chapter (without chapter3-final-FINAL.docx)
item.description:
Every writer who revises ends up with a folder like this:

chapter3.docx
chapter3-v2.docx
chapter3-tighter.docx
chapter3-final.docx
chapter3-final-FINAL.docx
chapter3-final-FINAL-use-this-one.docx

It happens because revision is experiment. You want to try the tighter opening without losing the old one, in case the old one was better. The files are a way of keeping your nerve.

The trouble is that they’re blind. You can’t see what changed between v2 and “tighter”, you can’t put the tighter opening in the book and the old ending alongside it, and three months later you can’t remember which one you liked.

item.title: Read your writing aloud: what your ear catches that your eyes miss
item.description:
Every editing guide says it: read your work aloud. It’s the one piece of advice that every writer agrees on, and the one most of us skip, because it’s slow, it’s a little embarrassing, and our voice gives out by chapter four.

It’s worth finding a way to do it anyway. Here’s why it works, and how to get the benefit without reading 90,000 words out loud yourself.

Why your ear catches what your eyes miss

When you reread your own writing silently, you read what you meant, not what you wrote. Your brain knows the sentence and fills it in. A missing “the”, a doubled word, a sentence that changed halfway through a revision: your eye slides right over them.

item.title: Story order vs. telling order: keeping a nonlinear timeline straight
item.description:
Every story has two orders.

There’s the order things happened: the soldier buys the paw in India, the Whites wish on it, the son dies at the factory, the knock comes at the door. And there’s the order you tell them in. Maybe you open on the knock and reach back for the rest.

Narrative theory calls these fabula (the story as it happened) and syuzhet (the story as told). You don’t need the Russian to use the idea, but you do need to keep the two apart, because almost every continuity error in a nonlinear book comes from mixing them up.

item.title: Accessibility
item.description:
We want WRITEpad and this website to be usable by everyone, and aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at level AA.

On this site that means text that meets AA contrast in light and dark mode, a skip link, navigation that works from the keyboard, visible focus, and images described for screen readers.

In the app, narration can read any manuscript aloud, dictation lets you write by voice, and themes, including custom colours with a contrast warning, let you set the page the way you read best.

item.title: Privacy
item.description:
The short version: your writing never comes to us. WRITEpad has no accounts, no analytics and no telemetry, and this website sets no cookies.

The app

WRITEpad works on a folder on your own computer. Your manuscripts, notes, versions, history and Library measurements stay in that folder, and we have no copy of them.

The app connects to the internet only when you ask it to:

  • Setting up narration downloads the Kokoro voice engine (from the Python Package Index) and its voice files (from GitHub).
  • Dictation downloads a Whisper speech model the first time you use it. Speech is transcribed on your computer.
  • Adding a script to the Library from a link fetches that page.
  • Polish with Claude is off by default. If you turn it on, dictated text is sent to Anthropic with your own API key, under Anthropic’s privacy policy.
  • Agents you connect through the MCP server act under their own provider’s terms.

This website

This website sets no cookies. We count visits with Zero Trust Analytics (ztas.io). It sets no cookies, stores nothing on your device and does not store your IP address. For each page view it records the page, the site that sent you here, your browser, device type and operating system, an approximate location (country, region and city), and a one-way code that changes every day so a visit isn’t counted twice.

item.title: Terms of use
item.description:
The software

WRITEpad is open-source software. Its source code is published on GitHub under the license in that repository, which governs how you may use, copy, change and share the code.

The software is provided as is, without warranty of any kind. Keep backups of work that matters to you; WRITEpad’s history feature and your own backups are the best protection against loss.

Your writing

What you write with WRITEpad is yours. We claim no rights to it, and we never receive it. The same goes for every ebook and audiobook you export.
